mcqs.question: The sliding-window solution for the longest substring without repeating characters uses two indices and a Set. What is its time complexity, and why?
options: O(n): each unit is inserted into the Set at most once and removed at most once, so the total work of both loops together is bounded by a constant per unit.
O(n²): a while loop is nested inside the for loop, so the worst case is n times n iterations.
O(n log n): Set operations cost log n on average and there are n of them.
O(min(n, distinct units)): the running time matches the Set's size bound.
mcqs.explanation: Correct because the left index never moves backwards: every shrink of the window consumes work that was prepaid by an earlier insertion, so each unit is added and removed at most once and the nested shape still amortizes to O(n). The strongest distractor is option 1: multiplying loop counts is only valid when the inner loop can restart from scratch on every outer iteration, which the monotonic left pointer makes impossible. Option 3 quotes the space bound, O(min(n, distinct-unit-count)), not the time bound.

mcqs.question: For a search box that may receive multi-code-point emoji, what does Array.from(text) give the longest-unique-substring algorithm, and what does it still not give?
options: Unicode code points, one per element; it does not segment grapheme clusters, so one user-perceived character can occupy several elements.
UTF-16 code units, exactly like direct string indexing, so surrogate pairs are split into two elements.
Grapheme clusters, one per user-perceived character, because Array.from splits text on perceived boundaries.
The same count as text.length: both count UTF-16 code units, so the choice cannot change the result.
mcqs.explanation: Correct: Array.from iterates code points, the safe default over raw indexing, but an emoji with a skin-tone modifier or a ZWJ sequence is several code points, so grapheme-level uniqueness needs a separate segmentation step and must be clarified as a requirement. The strongest distractor is option 2, which overcredits Array.from: it stops at code points and knows nothing about user-perceived boundaries. Option 1 describes direct string indexing, and option 3 wrongly assumes text.length counts what Array.from yields.

mcqs.question: Records arrive from several paginated responses, each parsed separately, so the same record can appear as two distinct objects. Which implementation dedupes by id, keeps the first-seen record and its position, and runs in O(n) average time?
options: return [...new Set(records)]: Set stores unique values and iterates in insertion order.
Filter with a Set of ids: skip a record whose id is already present, otherwise add the id and keep the record.
Sort the records by id, then remove adjacent duplicates.
Filter with a nested scan: keep a record only if no previously kept record has the same id.
mcqs.explanation: Correct: an explicit stable key (id) with Set membership gives O(n) average time and preserves first-seen order, which is exactly the bank's pattern. The strongest distractor is option 0: everything stated about Set is true (unique values, insertion order), but membership uses identity-based equality, so two separately created object literals with identical fields are both kept and nothing is deduped. Option 2 breaks the first-seen-position requirement and costs O(n log n); option 3 produces correct output but degrades to O(n²) on large merges.

mcqs.question: In a large breadth-first DOM traversal, why does the queue use a head index that only advances, instead of Array.shift()?
options: shift() removes from the wrong end for a FIFO queue, so the traversal order would become depth-first.
shift() is deprecated and scheduled for removal from the language.
shift()'s removal cost is linear in the remaining array, so a large traversal pays quadratic queue costs; the head index makes each dequeue O(1).
Arrays cannot shrink once allocated, so shift() only nulls the first slot and leaks it.
mcqs.explanation: Correct: shift() reindexes every remaining element, so removing n items one at a time costs O(n²) in queue operations; keeping a head index makes each dequeue O(1) and the whole traversal O(v + e). The strongest distractor is option 0: shift() is the correct FIFO end semantically, the problem is purely its cost, and confusing the two would point the fix in the wrong direction. Option 3 invents a memory model; shift() copies the remainder, it does not just null a slot.

mcqs.question: Which statement about memoizing an expensive derived value for a filterable list is correct?
options: Memoization makes the first computation cheaper by caching partial results during the initial run.
A Map keyed by the argument's identity stays correct even if callers mutate the argument between calls, because Map re-hashes the contents on lookup.
Memoization avoids repeating work for inputs already seen; it does not make the first computation cheaper and does not replace rendering only the rows that are needed.
An unbounded cache is safe for free-text query keys because Map evicts stale entries with LRU behavior.
mcqs.explanation: Correct, and it is the bank's exact caution: a cache only pays off on repeated inputs, so cold queries are as slow as before, and caching a derived array does nothing about rendering thousands of DOM rows. The strongest distractor is option 1: Map keys use identity-based equality, so a mutated-but-same-reference argument is a cache hit that returns stale data; the key must represent every input affecting the result, via immutable inputs or explicit versioning. Option 3 invents eviction: Map has none, which is why unbounded keys must be bounded by design.

mcqs.question: Choose the rate-limiting tool: (1) a search box where only the settled query should hit the API; (2) a scroll handler where the UI should update at a regular cadence while scrolling continues. Which pairing is right?
options: Throttle the search and debounce the scroll.

Debounce the search and throttle the scroll: debounce waits until calls stop for the delay so only the settled query fires; throttle permits at most one invocation per interval so updates stay regular.
Debounce both: debounce is the stricter, more modern option and subsumes throttle.
Use requestAnimationFrame for both: rAF is a rate limiter with a configurable interval.
mcqs.explanation: Correct: the definitions map directly onto the requirements; search needs the settled value (debounce waits until calls have stopped for the delay) and continuous scroll needs regular updates (throttle allows at most one invocation per interval). The strongest distractor is option 0, which inverts the criterion: it would hit the API on every keystroke bucket and starve scroll updates until scrolling stops entirely. Option 3 mislabels rAF: it aligns work with frames and has no configurable interval; the guidance is to batch scroll reads and writes in rAF in addition to keeping the handler light, not to use rAF as a debounce or throttle.

mcqs.question: Which set of values can structuredClone() copy in a browser but a JSON.parse(JSON.stringify()) round trip cannot preserve?
options: A function and a live DOM element node.
A Map with entries, a circular reference, and a Date object.
A Promise and a WeakMap.
None: both approaches clone exactly the same value graph and differ only in speed.
mcqs.explanation: Correct: structuredClone makes a deep copy that preserves circular references and keeps structured-cloneable values like Maps intact, while the JSON round trip is serialization: Map and Set entries are dropped (they stringify to {}), Dates come back as strings, and cycles throw a TypeError. The strongest distractor is option 0: functions and many DOM nodes are precisely the values that make structuredClone throw DataCloneError, since it is not a universal clone. Option 3 misses that the two algorithms only agree on the plain-JSON subset of the value graph.

mcqs.question: A route runs three independent fetches under Promise.all and one rejects. What happens to the other two network requests?
options: They are cancelled automatically: Promise.all's rejection propagates to sibling promises.
They keep running to completion; the rejection only abandons waiting for them, and cancelling them requires an AbortSignal passed to each fetch.
They are paused until the rejection is handled, then resumed or cancelled by the handler.
They resolve normally but Promise.all discards their results, which amounts to the same thing as cancelling them.
mcqs.explanation: Correct: Promise.all preserves input order and rejects on the first rejection, but rejection does not cancel the remaining operations; without signals the siblings still consume bandwidth and resolve into nothing. The strongest distractor is option 3: it is half right (their results are indeed discarded) and draws the wrong conclusion, since the requests still complete and the wasted work is observable on the network. Option 0 is the classic conflation of fail-fast observation with cancellation, the exact mix-up of concurrency, cancellation, and stale-result protection the bank warns about.

mcqs.question: What is the output order of: console.log('task start'); queueMicrotask(() => console.log('microtask')); setTimeout(() => console.log('timer task'), 0); console.log('task end');?
options: task start, microtask, task end, timer task
task start, task end, timer task, microtask
task start, task end, microtask, timer task
task start, timer task, task end, microtask
mcqs.explanation: Correct: the two synchronous logs run first; after the current task finishes the browser drains the microtask queue before returning to the event loop, so the microtask runs before the zero-delay timer task, exactly the bank's example. The strongest distractor is option 0: it assumes queueMicrotask runs its callback inline at the enqueue point, which would make microtasks indistinguishable from synchronous code. Option 1 reverses the drain rule by letting a task (the timer) run before pending microtasks, and option 2 treats setTimeout(..., 0) as synchronous.

mcqs.question: In a TreeWalker, an element matches the private-subtree rule. What is the difference between returning FILTER_REJECT and FILTER_SKIP for that element?
options: REJECT excludes the element and its entire subtree; SKIP excludes only the element and still visits its children.
REJECT aborts the whole traversal with an error; SKIP is the safe non-throwing variant.
They are equivalent for elements; the constants only differ for text and comment nodes.
SKIP excludes the element's subtree while REJECT excludes only the element itself.
mcqs.explanation: Correct: the bank's walker returns FILTER_REJECT for a private element precisely so its descendants are excluded, while non-target elements get FILTER_SKIP so traversal still descends into them. The strongest distractor is option 3, which inverts the semantics and would leak private text exactly like the naive simplification. Option 2 is plausible because the two constants do behave the same for NodeIterator (children are still visited), but for TreeWalker the subtree pruning is the entire point of REJECT.

scenarios.prompt: A dashboard route runs loadDashboard() on entry, may unmount before the fetches finish, and can be re-entered quickly. (1) Name every correctness and efficiency problem in this code. (2) Rewrite it so the three resources load concurrently, obsolete results can never render, and navigation cancels work. (3) State what changes if partial data is useful.
rubric: Identifies the waterfall: independent operations awaited one by one instead of started together, so latency sums.
Uses Promise.all for all-or-nothing loading and can state its exact semantics: preserves input order, rejects on first rejection, does not cancel the remaining operations.
Adds cancellation: one AbortSignal passed to every fetch, abort() on route change and cleanup, AbortError treated as expected rather than an error.
Guards rendering with request identity (current controller or version), so a slower obsolete load cannot overwrite newer data even while the component is still mounted.
Knows the partial-data alternative: Promise.allSettled with per-outcome rendering, and checks response.ok before parsing.

scenarios.prompt: This utility ships in a widget bundle. (1) List every defect in debounce and in how it is applied to the search input and the scroll badge. (2) Write a production version and spell out its API contract. (3) Explain what to do differently for the scroll badge and on component teardown.
rubric: Spots that arguments (and this) are dropped: the trailing call invokes fn with none of the handler's values.
Adds cancel() clearing the timer and requires calling it on teardown so no trailing call survives unmount and the closure stops retaining stale work.
States the leading/trailing and maxWait decisions explicitly instead of silently shipping trailing-only, and treats the interval as a product decision.
For the scroll badge, replaces timer-only debouncing with a light handler plus requestAnimationFrame-batched read/write: frame alignment, not just call rate.
Can justify debounce for search (only the settled query matters) versus throttle for continuous scroll, resize, or pointer work (at most one invocation per interval).

scenarios.prompt: mergePages combines users from several paginated API responses; the same user can appear on more than one page, and each page is parsed separately, so duplicates are distinct objects. (1) Explain precisely why the current implementation removes nothing. (2) Rewrite it so the last-seen record wins while every id stays at the position where it was first seen. (3) State the complexity and what you would ask the product owner first.
rubric: Explains the identity-versus-structural failure precisely: Set keeps both separately parsed objects because object values compare by reference, not by structure.
Keys by the stable id and states the conflict rule (last-wins here) before or while coding.
Knows Map re-set semantics: the value is replaced while the key keeps its first-insertion position, yielding last-wins values in first-seen order.
States O(n) average time and O(n) additional space, and avoids sort-then-dedupe, which breaks first-seen order and costs O(n log n).

scenarios.prompt: The team uses this to prefetch a list of pages with limit 3. A caller asserts that results arrive in input order and the assertion fails intermittently. (1) Explain the order bug and why it is intermittent. (2) The utility also silently misbehaves for some limit values and has an unstated failure contract; identify both. (3) Fix the code and write down the guarantees the fixed version gives.
rubric: Diagnoses the order bug: push-in-completion-order versus assignment at the original index, and explains the intermittency (it depends on task timing).
Preserves the at-most-limit invariant with the worker-pool pull loop rather than starting all tasks at once.
Validates the limit as a positive integer instead of silently returning wrong output for 0, negatives, or fractions.
States the failure contract: fail-fast rejection leaves in-flight tasks running (observed, not cancelled), or offers per-item outcomes or AbortSignal-based cancellation.
Notes what the limit does and does not promise: caps simultaneous resource use; no throughput guarantee, no faster individual tasks.
